dossier.identity_policy: Solvent and extractant IDs are independent benchmark-only labels and do not identify real materials. Equal codes across the two fields have no meaning.

# Partition study hypotheses

## Pre-experiment expectations

**H1 [tentative] — material pairing.** The solvent–extractant pair will control the equilibrium target distribution, with interactions possible. From the marginal dossier only, S2 and X2 are expected to be comparatively favorable, but no claim about the best pair is justified. Controlled single-factor screens around S2/X2 and a repeat will test this.

**H2 [tentative] — phase amounts.** At fixed pairing and mixing, increasing the organic share of total liquid should increase the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory found in organic phase. A distribution-ratio model predicts dependence on both material-specific affinity and actual organic/aqueous volumes, not on aqueous addition alone.

**H3 [tentative] — mixing.** Insufficient mixing may leave transfer below equilibrium; beyond adequate mixing, increasing time/speed should have little effect. Low, standard, and high mixing conditions will test this, though time and speed are jointly varied and therefore not separately identifiable.

Plan: use pre-separation HPLC in all 12 independent batches to observe both phases, then retain a prespecified phase, terminate, and final-assay every batch. Differences will be interpreted against reported instrument uncertainty and replication, not merely numerical rank.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 — material pairing [supported in screened scope, interaction unresolved]
At standard composition (0.04 L solvent, 0.02 L extractant, 0.04 L aqueous addition) and 120 s/600 rpm mixing, material choice materially changes pre-separation organic target fraction beyond the HPLC 0.015 standard uncertainty. With X2, observed organic fractions were about 0.259 (S0), 0.343 (S1), 0.260 (S2), and 0.378 (S3) (events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037). With S2, X0/X1/X2/X3 gave about 0.284/0.303/0.260/0.372 (events -0047, -0057, -0027, -0067). Thus the dossier marginal tendency did not reliably predict these controlled pair-specific results; S2/X2 was not comparatively favorable in this slice. Only row/column screens were performed, so the full interaction table remains unidentified.

The S2/X2 standard repeat gave organic fractions 0.260 and 0.280 and aqueous fractions 0.735 and 0.696 (events -0027 and -0077), broadly consistent given independent HPLC uncertainties and imperfect observed closure, but only two replicates limit variance assessment.

**Testable consequence:** if pairing effects reflect equilibrium affinity, material-related changes should persist when actual phase ratio is accounted for. A full factorial or selected cross-pair (e.g. S3/X3) would distinguish additive marginal effects from solvent–extractant interaction.

## H2 — phase amounts [tentative]
A distribution-ratio relationship should use measured phase ratio rather than nominal additions because standard batches show measured organic phase ratios near 0.18–0.22 despite 0.04 L solvent + 0.02 L extractant versus 0.04 L aqueous addition. The next low/high composition tests are prospective tests of monotonicity.

## H3 — mixing [tentative]
Insufficient mixing may reduce transfer; a plateau is expected at adequate mixing. Low and high joint time/speed settings remain to be tested, with joint variation preventing attribution to one mixing variable.

## Phase-retention interpretation [supported]
Separation retains the requested phase rather than switching the measurement source. Organic-retained final assays track pre-separation organic target fractions (e.g. events -0017 to -0020 and -0067 to -0070); aqueous-retained assays instead report high aqueous inventory (events -0007 to -0010 and -0077 to -0080). Small apparent content in the removed phase is compatible with assay noise/sampling, not evidence that removal failed. Phase choice must therefore follow which inventory is desired, not phase_ratio alone.

notes.text:
# Partition study — finalized source-stage hypotheses

## H1 — material pairing [supported in screened scope; interaction unresolved]
At standard composition (0.04 L solvent, 0.02 L extractant, 0.04 L aqueous addition) and 120 s/600 rpm mixing, material choice changed pre-separation organic target inventory by more than the HPLC 0.015 standard uncertainty. With X2, organic fractions were about 0.259/0.343/0.260/0.378 for S0/S1/S2/S3 (runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037). With S2, X0/X1/X2/X3 gave 0.284/0.303/0.260/0.372 (-0047, -0057, -0027, -0067). The marginal dossier did not reliably identify the observed pair behavior; S2/X2 was not especially favorable in this controlled slice. Because only one solvent column and one extractant row were screened, a full interaction surface and untested cross-pairs remain unidentified.

S2/X2 standard repeats gave organic fractions 0.260 and 0.280 and aqueous fractions 0.735 and 0.696 (-0027, -0077). They are broadly compatible with the stated HPLC uncertainties but two replicates do not establish process variance.

**Consequence:** pair-specific effects should persist under replicated matched phase ratios. Selected cross-pairs or a full factorial would distinguish additive marginal effects from interactions.

## H2 — phase amounts [supported for explicit phase addition; simple constant-D model unresolved]
Changing only nominal solvent/aqueous additions from 0.02/0.06 through 0.04/0.04 to 0.06/0.02 at fixed 0.02 L extractant did not materially change measured phase ratio or organic inventory: measured ratios stayed about 0.18–0.21 and organic fractions about 0.26–0.31 (-0027, -0077, -0087, -0097). This demonstrates why solvent addition and aqueous addition cannot be treated as the complete organic and aqueous phase volumes.

By contrast, an explicit 0.06 L organic-phase addition with 0.02 L solvent and 0.02 L extractant produced measured phase ratio 0.795 and organic target fraction 0.799 (-0117), far from the standard condition. Thus the measured phase ratio is strongly predictive within this intervention, and actual phase-forming additions matter. However, back-calculated distribution-ratio proxies from two standard repeats and the explicit-organic case are roughly 1.38, 1.85, and 0.91, so a single constant affinity coefficient is not established. Possible reasons include formulation-dependent affinity/extractant dilution, process variability, and noisy/nonclosing sampled inventories.

**Consequence:** additional replicated phase-ratio levels created by explicit aqueous/organic additions are needed before fitting a volume law. Predictions should use measured or composition-derived actual phase volumes, not nominal aqueous addition alone.

## H3 — mixing [no detected effect in tested range; plateau hypothesis unresolved]
At S2/X2 standard composition, low mixing (10 s, 100 rpm) gave pre-separation organic fraction 0.271 and phase ratio 0.213 (-0107), similar to standard repeats (0.260 and 0.280; -0027, -0077). The numerical differences are comparable with HPLC uncertainty and limited repeatability evidence, so no mixing effect was detected. This is consistent with rapid equilibration or a plateau already reached at the low setting, but it does not prove mixing independence. Time and speed were jointly changed, only one low run was performed, and no unmixed or independent time/speed series was tested.

## Phase retention [supported]
Pre-separation HPLC is the appropriate two-phase reading. After `separate_phase`, final assay reports the retained phase: organic retention preserved approximately the pre-separation organic inventory, while aqueous-retained batches reported high aqueous inventory and near-zero organic signal within assay noise (-0007 to -0010; -0077 to -0080). Therefore retention must be selected according to the target inventory in each phase. `phase_ratio` is a volume fraction, not target recovery, and missing/noisy closure must not be interpreted as zero or exact loss.

## Limits
Twelve batches supported controlled row/column material screens, two standard repeats, phase-composition contrasts, one explicit-organic intervention, and one low-mixing test. Evidence is synthetic and anonymous, full pairwise interactions were not mapped, phase-volume response lacks replicated levels, mixing time and speed are confounded, and observed target-fraction sums can deviate from one because of sampling/noise. No unobserved component is inferred as zero.

payload.report:
Observations: All 12 batches used 0.020 mol reagent and pre-separation HPLC, followed by phase separation and a final assay. Under the standard recipe (0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L aqueous phase, 0.020 L extractant; 120 s at 600 rpm), material labels affected partition. With X2 fixed, batches 1–4 gave HPLC organic-target fractions of about 0.259, 0.343, 0.260 and 0.378 for S0–S3, respectively. With S2 fixed, batches 5, 6, 3 and 7 gave about 0.284, 0.303, 0.260 and 0.372 for X0–X3. Thus S3/X2 and S2/X3 were stronger within their respective one-dimensional screens, while S2/X2 was not. Standard S2/X2 repeats, batches 3 and 8, gave organic fractions 0.260 and 0.280 and aqueous fractions 0.735 and 0.696; this is reasonable repeat agreement given HPLC standard uncertainties of 0.015 per target channel, although two runs cannot characterize process variance.

Phase-amount observations: In batches 9, 3/8 and 10, changing solvent/aqueous additions from 0.020/0.060 through 0.040/0.040 to 0.060/0.020 L, while holding extractant at 0.020 L, left measured phase ratios near 0.18–0.21 and organic-target fractions near 0.26–0.31. These nominal additions therefore did not behave as direct measures of final organic and aqueous phase volumes. Batch 12 instead explicitly added 0.060 L of organic phase with 0.020 L solvent and 0.020 L X2. Its measured phase ratio rose to 0.795, with organic and aqueous target fractions of 0.799 and 0.226. After retaining the organic phase, its final assay found 0.778 organic target. This is a large, unambiguous phase-amount response.

Mixing observation: Batch 11 used only 10 s at 100 rpm at the standard S2/X2 composition. It gave phase ratio 0.213 and organic target 0.271, similar to the two standard-mixing replicates. No mixing effect was detected over this tested contrast.

Retention observations: Final assays behaved as assays of the requested retained phase. Examples of organic retention are batch 2 (HPLC organic 0.343; final 0.342), batch 7 (0.372; final 0.369), and batch 12 (0.799; final 0.778). With aqueous retention, batch 1 changed from pre-separation aqueous 0.693 to final aqueous 0.743, and batch 8 from 0.696 to 0.750, while final organic signals were approximately zero. Accordingly, phase_ratio is a volume-related measurement, not itself target recovery; phase retention must follow the target inventory.

Inference: Partition is jointly controlled by material pairing and actual phase constitution. The explicit organic-phase intervention shows that increasing the realized organic phase can strongly increase organic target inventory. Material effects are also real within the screened row and column. A predictive account should therefore condition on solvent–extractant pairing and measured or otherwise validated phase volumes rather than equating nominal solvent addition with organic volume. Separation then selects which of the already partitioned inventories is retained.

The data do not establish a single constant distribution coefficient. A volume-corrected distribution-ratio proxy was approximately 1.38 and 1.85 in the two standard S2/X2 repeats but about 0.91 in the explicit-organic case. That variation could reflect formulation-dependent affinity or extractant dilution, but could also arise from process variability, measurement error, or imperfect closure of the separately reported target fractions. Thus a constant-affinity model is a useful candidate, not a demonstrated law.

Contribution of supplied information: The dossier correctly framed solvent and extractant as independent anonymous factors and warned that their interaction, phase-volume response and mixing response were undisclosed. Its marginal summaries suggested S2 and X2 might be favorable priors. Controlled experiments were essential because S2/X2 was not favorable in the tested local comparisons. This does not prove the dossier was wrong: marginal panel averages need not predict a particular pair, and the untested interaction matrix could reconcile both results.

Competing explanations and uncertain scope: The apparent material trends might be additive marginal effects or solvent–extractant interactions; only one solvent column and one extractant row were screened, so untested cross-pairs—including S3/X3—cannot be ranked. The phase response might follow equilibrium mass action, but batch 12 also changed formulation and extractant concentration relative to realized phase volume, confounding pure volume with composition. The absence of a mixing effect may mean equilibration was already rapid at 10 s/100 rpm, or that this assay lacked power to detect a modest kinetic effect; time and speed were varied together and only one low-mixing batch was run. Settling was fixed at 120 s, reagent loading was fixed, no unmixed condition was tested, and explicit phase-ratio levels were not replicated. Reported target fractions sometimes did not sum exactly to one, so missing inventory should not be interpreted as a new species or exact loss without further evidence. Conclusions apply only to these anonymous benchmark materials and tested operating range.

payload.rationale: I treated extractant volume as the organic-phase amount and solvent plus aqueous addition as the aqueous-phase amount, then used partition affinities estimated from the standard-volume screens. S2/X0 and S2/X3 are directly anchored by batches 5 and 7; S0/X0 and S0/X3 are wider extrapolations combining the S0-versus-S2 contrast at X2 with the X0/X3 contrasts at S2. The X3 advantage is supported by both the experiments and the supplied marginal information, so Q06 is favored over Q05. The low-mixing experiment showed no detectable deficit, so the long mixing schedules here are treated as equilibrated; remaining uncertainty covers sparse replication, unmeasured pair interactions, and scope of the phase-volume model.

payload.report:
1. The least-tested self-developed law is the additive pair-affinity extrapolation used for unmeasured S0/X0 and S0/X3 combinations. Batches 1–4 measured only the X2 solvent column, while batches 3 and 5–7 measured only the S2 extractant row; no experiment directly tested whether the X3-over-X0 effect observed with S2 transfers unchanged to S0. The related assumption that extractant volume equals organic-phase volume while solvent plus aqueous addition equals aqueous-phase volume is plausible from batches 9, 10 and 12, but was not calibrated at the smaller prediction volumes. An instance-specific marginal material dossier was supplied, but no complete pair table or fully specified instance law was supplied. The dossier’s marginal rankings were themselves weak predictors of the controlled S2/X2 result.

2. I would run the exact Q06 composition as a pre-registered cross-pair test: S0 (0.020 L), aqueous phase (0.015 L), X3 (0.019 L), 900 s at 1200 rpm, then 300 s settling. Before any phase removal I would measure HPLC target fractions and phase_ratio. The additive equilibrium explanation predicts roughly 0.57 organic target and a realized organic volume fraction near 0.35. A result near those values would support transferring the X3 advantage from batch 7 to S0 and strengthen the Q06-over-Q05 decision. An organic fraction near the S0/X0 prediction (~0.46), or below it, would indicate a strong S0–X3 interaction and make that decision uncertain or reverse it. A target split inconsistent with the measured phase_ratio would instead weaken the simple volume-law interpretation and favor composition-dependent affinity or incomplete equilibration.

3. The measured phase_ratio evidence was underused. Standard batches showed appreciable scatter around the nominal 0.20 organic fraction, and batch 12 provided only one explicit-organic level. The predictions nevertheless used nominal component-volume accounting rather than a fitted relationship between additions and realized phase volumes. The final-assay comparisons, impurity/purity shifts after retaining different phases, and imperfect pre-separation target closure were also used mainly as qualitative checks rather than incorporated quantitatively. The supplied marginal dossier could have been used more formally as a shrinkage prior, although its mismatch with the local screens argues against giving it high weight.

The least reliable predictions are Q03, Q04 and Q06 because S0/X3 was unobserved, followed by Q01, Q02, Q05, Q09 and Q10 because S0/X0 was also inferred rather than measured. Q02 and Q04 additionally extrapolate to an extractant amount above the campaign’s 0.020 L standard. Q11 versus Q12 is uncertain because mixing speed was never varied independently, although their long durations make a large difference less likely. Q01’s aqueous-retention decision is more robust than its exact fractions because the predicted split is far from 50:50.

There is a real methodological tension between the sealed report and predictions: the report said that a single constant distribution coefficient was not established and that actual phase volumes should be measured or validated, whereas the predictions used an equilibrium affinity model with deterministic volume bookkeeping. Wider intervals partly acknowledged that extrapolation but did not remove the inconsistency. Exact complementarity of the predicted noiseless fractions is not by itself inconsistent with the report—the report attributed much of the observed nonclosure to sampling/noise—but it assumes no true loss of target inventory, which the campaign did not independently prove.
